chapter: Regional bands, politics and travel abroad
title: Dignity versus the handkerchief-head stereotype
summary: Wilson discusses how film parts forced the clown image on black performers, naming Lena Horne and Billy Eckstine, and Hampton and Armstrong as showmen.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That is a serious problem. A lot of performers, Negro performers in the past -- I've sat in on meetings on this question where I've heard, actually, some of the people who've made some movies years ago, that if they don't behave that way -- that's the parts they write for them and if they don't behave that way, they're not going to get the job. We used to call them the Uncle Tom or the handkerchief head type of performer; that's all the parts they wrote for them.
I think the first Negro presented with any kind of dignity at all might have been -- what was that girl's name?

Freddie Washington in "Imitation of Life", Claudette Colbert's half sister or something -- I didn't see the movie. And then later Lena Horne, I think, was presented pretty good in the movies during the second World War.
Well, that may be true for movies but what about music --

And there wasn't a ballad singer who came to the top until Billy Eckstein. You know, Billy Daniels was singing those ballads long before Eckstein and couldn't get to first base. All the fans would come to Harlem to hear Billy Daniels sing in a dive before he went baritone and shot up like magic. But Billy Eckstein got big just singing romantic ballads (inaudible) in New York. Just like Frank Sinatra or something.

But see, times change. And back in those days, of course, I was fortunate with that Goodman thing to be able to perform with dignity and get in the top world of publicity and before a big, mass public with Goodman. And with that sort of organization, it was perfect for me to be that way, you know.
Jackie Robinson wasn't no clown out there either, was he?
No, not at all. Not at all.
But (Inaudible) but you didn't have to do that then.
No, but Lionel (Hampton) was a natural showman,
you know. Lionel actually enjoys -- he has a ball, you know, putting on quite an act along with his music. Juggling those sticks, you know, he gets a kick out of that.
Well, I could say the same thing for Louis Armstrong, too. He enjoys that little cliché thing, or something. But it could be interpreted as the other way.
